title: Identical twins share their DNA, but not their fingerprints
body: The ridges on your fingertips are laid down in the womb, at around the **15th week** of fetal development, and they last until after death. Genes set the general type of pattern, which is why identical twins have very similar prints. But tiny differences in each fingertip's surroundings while the ridges form add details of their own, so even twins with the same DNA end up with prints that are not identical. How much comes from genes and how much from the environment is still unclear.

slides.question: Which fingerprint pattern is the most common?
slides.explanation: Loops make up about 60 to 65% of all fingerprints, whorls about 30 to 35%, and arches only about 5%.

slides.heading: Roughly 6 in 10 fingerprints are loops
slides.note: Loops are about 60–65% of fingerprints, whorls 30–35% and arches about 5%

slides.caption: William Herschel, who began fingerprinting in India in 1858, compared prints of the same fingers taken decades apart. The ridges had not changed.

slides.prompt: Galton worked out the odds of two different people having matching prints. What did he get?
slides.detail: His statistical model was an early estimate. Academics today still question the error rates and statistics behind fingerprint matching.
